The maturation of high-throughput biology over the past two decades has transformed multi-omics from an opportunistic by-product of profiling a sample with several platforms into an explicit analytical discipline. Where early studies tended to concatenate single-omics outputs at the level of figures or supplementary tables, contemporary cohort and single-cell studies increasingly benefit from modelling molecular layers jointly so that shared regulatory programmes, modality-specific responses and missing-data patterns can be disentangled in a principled way [R2, R5, R40]. This shift has been driven by a steady expansion in the layers that can be measured routinely — bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and spatial modalities — and by the recognition that most biologically interesting phenotypes arise from interactions across these layers rather than from any one in isolation. The reviews cited above collectively illustrate the breadth of the modality catalogue now in routine use [R55, R56, R59]; the specific inventory supported by any given tool is far narrower, and no single platform delivers all of them. The empirical evidence that integration outperforms well-designed single-omics analysis is itself context-dependent: a recent colorectal cancer benchmark comparing eight unsupervised integrative clustering methods on simulated and real TCGA data reported that similarity-network fusion produced the best subtype classification accuracy among them, but performance was sensitive to the simulated correlation structure and no method dominated across all metrics, illustrating that added layers do not automatically deliver added insight [R17]. Integration, in other words, is not an end in itself; it is a methodological choice whose value must be defended against well-controlled unimodal alternatives.

The practical consequences of treating integration as a discipline rather than a postscript are now visible across the software landscape. Generic spreadsheets and monolithic pipelines struggle on three fronts simultaneously: sample coverage is rarely balanced across modalities, data formats are heterogeneous even within a single project, and the analytical workflows required to move from raw features to interpretable models are long enough that their conclusions are sensitive to undocumented parameter choices [R1, R10]. The result is a well-documented reproducibility crisis in which re-running a published multi-omics analysis rarely yields identical biological conclusions, even when the input data are unchanged. This concern is sharpened in microbiome and host-microbiome settings, where metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, metabolomic and host-response layers each have their own conventions, ontologies and batch-effect structures that must be reconciled before any joint modelling is meaningful [R1, R39]. The concern is sharpened further still in clinical cohorts, where the cost of re-analysis mistakes is highest and where standards such as FAIR data objects and reproducible workflow runtimes — declarative pipeline managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow that orchestrate multi-step analyses under a single definition — are now expected rather than aspirational [R27].

Closely connected to this shift, software itself has become a first-class research output: methods papers now routinely compete on the basis of architectural choices — whether a tool exposes a unified multi-assay data structure [R45], whether it scales to single-cell modalities [R4, R13, R26], whether it can be replayed through a workflow manager [R27, R43], or whether it offers a graphical interface that lets clinician-scientists participate without writing code [R9, R16, R23, R41]. At the same time, the proliferation of specialised tools has produced a fragmentation problem: a typical integrative analysis can plausibly call on a matrix-factorization method, a network-based meta-analyser, a pathway-level integrator and a deep-learning embedder, yet there is little consensus on how these pieces should be composed, and the conceptual framework that ties them together is often left implicit [R40]. In our view, even when a conceptual scheme exists, its assumptions about independence between modalities, sparsity of the signal and tolerance for missing data are not always made visible to the user, which complicates both interpretation and reuse.

This review therefore treats software as the primary object of comparison. We survey general-purpose integration frameworks and methods, microbiome-centred tools, web servers and point-and-click platforms, and the data structures and workflow systems that underpin reproducibility, before focusing in detail on EasyMultiProfiler (EMP), a recently published R workflow that uses the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment classes to deliver a five-module pipeline — extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation — for microbiome and host-microbiome studies [R1]. Throughout, we apply a consistent comparative lens that asks what each tool assumes about the data, what integration strategy it implements, what evidence supports its performance claims, and how those claims are qualified when examined critically. The goal is not to rank tools, but to make the design space legible so that users and developers can choose — or build — software whose assumptions match the biological question at hand.

The literature on multi-omics integration has converged, almost by convention, into a three-stage taxonomy that distinguishes the moment at which information from multiple assays is combined. In the early-integration paradigm, also termed concatenation-based integration, features from all omics layers are merged into a single design matrix and analysed with one model that treats features as exchangeable predictors under the assumption of joint observation over the same samples. The mixOmics R package provides a canonical realisation through sparse PLS and its multi-block extension DIABLO, in which partial least-squares components are fitted on concatenated feature matrices and forced to be correlated across blocks through a design matrix [R3, R44]. MixMC provides a multivariate statistical framework that accounts for the compositional nature of 16S rRNA marker-gene data and supports multi-block integration across body sites [R64], and the regularised multi-block family represented by RGCCA/SGCCA consolidates block-specific latent components for exploratory integration of multi-block datasets through generalised canonical correlation analysis [R65]. A persistent weakness of this class is that it imposes a single metric and a single noise model on layers whose scales, sparsity and dependence structures differ profoundly; pre-processing choices therefore dominate downstream conclusions, and the literature is conspicuously thin on systematic comparisons of those choices.

Intermediate integration postpones the moment of fusion. Joint dimensionality reduction and matrix or tensor factorisations infer a small set of latent variables that approximate all omics matrices simultaneously: MOFA is the canonical example, using a Bayesian factor-analysis framework whose factors are shared across modalities and are interpretable in terms of both common and assay-specific variance [R2]; its single-cell extension MOFA+ applies the same logic through variational inference and flexible sparsity priors to multi-modal single-cell data [R4]. Related matrix-factorisation-based clustering methods, including multi-layer NMF, semi-supervised deep NMF (SSD-MO), MOTL's transfer-learning extension of MOFA and MLMF, similarly factorise modalities into shared and residual components [R12, R19, R50]. Network-based intermediate integration offers a geometric alternative: Similarity Network Fusion constructs a sample-similarity graph per modality and fuses them through message-passing to produce a single affinity matrix usable for clustering [R5]; MUUMI extends this paradigm by coupling SNF with interactome inference to identify molecular signatures, although its validation so far has been limited to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and macrophage models [R10]. The advantage over concatenation is that each modality retains its own geometry; the disadvantage is that the resulting latent space or fused graph no longer carries the original features, complicating biomarker attribution and forcing users into post-hoc loadings analyses.

Late, or decision-level, integration keeps each omics layer analytically separate until the very end, combining only outputs — predictions, scores or rankings — across modalities. The simplest realisation is an ensemble of single-omics classifiers whose votes are aggregated, but the literature now extends this idea to multi-modal Bayesian uncertainty estimation, as in TMODINET, where each omics-specific predictor contributes through Dempster–Shafer fusion rather than naive averaging [R24]. Late integration is the natural choice when modalities are simply not co-measured, when one modality is very small, or when each omics platform already has its own gold-standard pipeline whose parameters should not be perturbed. The cost is that cross-omics interactions inside a single sample cannot in principle be recovered without at least one intermediate step somewhere in the workflow.

Cutting across these three stages are two orthogonal axes that are often elided in tool papers. The first is supervision: MOFA is unsupervised [R2], DIABLO is supervised by design [R44], and a family of recent variational and supervised factor models, including SigMAE, explicitly couples dimensionality reduction with prediction in a single optimisation [R35]. The second axis is data-driven versus knowledge-driven integration. Data-driven methods seek latent structure without recourse to prior biology, and most factor and matrix-factorisation work, including MOFA and SNF, falls into this category [R2, R5]. Knowledge-driven approaches compress features into pathways, networks or curated ontologies before integration: PathIntegrate transforms molecular data to single-sample pathway scores and applies single- or multi-view predictive models on top [R30], while the OmicsNet module of the Analyst suite performs biological-network integration as a third step after single-omics and data-driven integration [R23].

The taxonomy, while pedagogically convenient, is not as crisp as the labels suggest. DIABLO is variously described as "early" and "intermediate" in different papers depending on whether the design matrix or the block structure is emphasised, and supervised variants of MOFA collapse the unsupervised/supervised axis onto what should be a separate methodological decision [R44, R2]. Terminology is also unstable across tool papers: "joint dimensionality reduction", "matrix factorisation", "multi-view learning" and "integration" are used almost interchangeably, which is one reason why head-to-head benchmarks frequently disagree on what counts as a baseline. More importantly, the practical choice among strategies is dictated less by algorithmic novelty than by data structure. Matched samples with low missingness favour intermediate factor or network fusion [R2, R5]; high sample-to-feature ratios favour concatenation or supervised PLS [R3, R44]; block-missing data almost force late integration or pathway-level aggregation [R30, R24]; and very small cohorts may require transfer-learning enhancements before any of the above will work reliably [R50]. These contingencies explain why no single dominant workflow has emerged from the methodological literature, and they caution against treating any one integration strategy as universally preferable.

Several widely used tools fall outside this three-stage scheme without distorting it, and we name them here to clarify the scope rather than dismiss them. Single-cell anchoring methods such as Seurat and the totalVI/scArches/UINMF family addressed cross-technology dataset alignment and missing-modality prediction in single-cell data, which is the primary concern of the benchmarking section rather than this taxonomy [R61, R26]. Microbiome-specific standards — MaAsLin2 and ANCOM-BC for differential abundance testing, and mixMC for compositional multi-block analysis — sit at a different level of the stack, providing components for integration rather than full integration strategies [R62, R63, R64]. Pathway-level web platforms such as 3Omics are subsumed under the knowledge-driven axis defined above [R66]. The taxonomy should be read as a navigation aid for the methods most often invoked in methodological reviews, not as a census of every tool that touches the problem, and our aim here has been to map strategies rather than to rank tools by depth of implementation.

General-purpose integrative frameworks for multi-omics data span at least four overlapping algorithmic lineages, each with a distinct conceptual take on what "integration" should mean. They differ sharply in input expectations, scalability, and what counts as a published tool versus a one-off pipeline, and a candid reading of the literature shows that the gap between methodological novelty and reproducible, well-engineered software remains large.

The factor-analysis lineage is dominated by Multi-Omics Factor Analysis and its descendants. The original MOFA infers a set of latent factors that capture both shared and modality-specific variation across heterogeneous omics layers and supports downstream tasks such as sample subgrouping and imputation [R2]; MOFA+ generalises this to multi-modal single-cell data using variational inference and flexible sparsity priors, allowing joint modelling across sample groups and modalities [R4]. A more recent addition is MOTL, a transfer-learning extension that augments MOFA-style joint matrix factorisation by borrowing latent factor structure from a large heterogeneous "learning" dataset to improve factorisation of limited-sample target data, with validation on simulated data and glioblastoma samples [R50]. The transfer-learning formulation is useful in settings with few samples, but its gain over plain MOFA is intrinsically tied to the relevance of the source dataset to the target — a dependence that is rarely probed in head-to-head terms and that cautions against uncritical adoption across biological domains.

The PLS-based integrative lineage is essentially the mixOmics family. mixOmics provides a coherent R package for feature selection, dimension reduction and integration of multiple omics assays through sparse PLS and related variants [R3]. Its supervised extension DIABLO identifies correlated subsets of discriminating molecular features across assays and phenotypic groups, offering modular and cross-over study designs and competitive predictive performance relative to supervised approaches while improving biological relevance over unsupervised integrative baselines [R44]. MixOmics has had demonstrable reach beyond cancer, including in plant abiotic-stress workflows for vertical and horizontal integration of phenomics, metabolomics, proteomics and transcriptomics [R33], which makes it one of the few general-purpose frameworks with broad-domain traction. Its main limitation is conceptual: linear projection in supervised mode can be sensitive to confounded designs, and feature selection on sparse PLS components remains a perennial source of reproducibility discussion.

A third lineage concentrates on similarity-network fusion. The canonical SNF method constructs per-data-type patient similarity networks and fuses them into one integrative network, achieving substantial gains over single-data-type analyses on five cancer datasets [R5]. MUUMI unifies statistical meta-analysis with network-based integration by combining SNF with interactome inference to identify robust molecular signatures, though its validation has so far been limited to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and THP-1 macrophages [R10]. DeepMoIC embeds SNF into a deep Graph Convolutional Network trained on autoencoder-extracted representations for cancer subtyping [R28], while MINGLE uses sparse network estimation to merge multi-omics information into an integrated network for glioma heterogeneity [R49]. The conceptual unity of this lineage is appealing, but fusion methods are highly sensitive to the choice of similarity metric and to the propagation of hub nodes, and most published implementations do not expose the network's sensitivity to these choices transparently.

Deep matrix and tensor factorisations form a fourth stream. SSD-MO combines semi-supervised learning with multi-layer deep non-negative matrix factorisation and reports 7–24 % F-score improvements over baselines on six TCGA cancer datasets — gains measured within the TCGA setting the authors themselves curated and whose generalisability is therefore uncertain [R12]; MLMF integrates multi-layer linear/nonlinear factorisation with consensus fusion and a class-indicator matrix to handle partially missing omics, benchmarked across twelve multi-omics cancer datasets [R19]. GeDGC learns shared latent representations together with cluster factors through Gaussian mixture priors while imposing a graph-embedding constraint to preserve cell-cell structure in single-cell multi-omics data [R13]. MCluster-VAEs further couples attention-based VAEs with a clustering objective, end-to-end, and is benchmarked against twelve other multi-omics clustering methods on TCGA datasets [R38]. These models are often impressive on TCGA but interpretability is uneven, and like most deep factorisations they inherit TCGA-tuned hyperparameters.

Graph-neural-network approaches are gaining ground. BioNeuralNet is presented as a modular Python framework for end-to-end network-based multi-omics analysis using GNNs to learn low-dimensional embeddings for downstream tasks [R11]. MOGOLA combines GCN/GAT intra-omics feature extraction with a gating and cross-omics attention fusion mechanism, reporting gains over eleven state-of-the-art methods on BRCA, KIPAN, ROSMAP and LGG benchmarks [R52]; MO-GCAN trains per-omics GCNs whose embeddings are concatenated and re-fused through a graph-attention sample network across eight cancer types [R47]. TMODINET couples self-attention with adaptive graph dynamic learning and Dirichlet/Dempster-Shafer uncertainty estimation for cancer diagnosis with explicit uncertainty quantification [R24]. Even the most carefully engineered GNN pipelines remain challenging to configure in low-data regimes, and current architectural diversity outpaces agreed-upon protocols.

Attention-based deep architectures and probabilistic models round out the catalogue. MOADLN applies self-attention to construct patient correlations before classification, outperforming several baselines on KIRP, KIRC and related TCGA multi-omics tasks [R34]; CAEncoder combines a Vision Transformer with CycleGAN in an end-to-end contrastive framework for cancer detection [R48]; MOKAN adapts Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with learnable edge-weight activations and subspace decomposition to capture inter-omics heterogeneity [R14]. On the probabilistic side, POPLS-DA provides a workflow that jointly analyses transcriptomics, proteomics and drug-screening data through a probabilistic PLS-DA formulation [R32]; NetMIM uses a spike-and-slab Bayesian prior with gene-pathway information and FBM-style data augmentation to handle block-missingness in multi-omics cohorts [R31]; PathIntegrate transforms multi-omics data to single-sample pathway scores before applying single- or multi-view predictive models [R30]; SigMAE fuses dimensionality reduction with predictive modelling in a supervised variational Bayesian factor setting [R35]; STATegra offers a conceptual multi-stage framework combining component analysis, non-parametric combination and exploratory analysis on TCGA glioblastoma and melanoma data [R40].

A complementary set of widely used tools sits outside the four lineages above but is routinely invoked alongside them. Seurat's anchor-based integration [R61] remains the single-cell standard across scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, spatial gene expression and protein measurements. For microbiome data, MaAsLin2 [R62] and ANCOM-BC [R63] supply multivariable and bias-corrected differential abundance testing, while the mixOmics variant mixMC adapts PLS-DA to compositional 16S data [R64]. Multi-block canonical correlation methods such as RGCCA/SGCCA offer a classical statistical alternative for block-structured multi-omics [R65], and 3Omics [R66] provides one-click correlation, co-expression and enrichment integration of human transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic data. Their omission from the algorithmic taxonomy is methodological: each addresses a narrower input/output contract than the end-to-end frameworks profiled here, and they are best read as composable components rather than competing replacements.

The critical reading that emerges is sobering. First, input expectations are highly heterogeneous: some tools expect matched-sample matrices, others expect graphs, others expect labelled and unlabelled samples simultaneously, which means their "head-to-head" comparison is often a category error. Second, despite the proliferation of methods, the recurring lack of independent, cross-domain head-to-head evaluation means that apparent superiority on TCGA is not yet transferable evidence; a recent benchmarking effort on unsupervised integrative clustering in TCGA colorectal cancer, for example, found SNF gave the best subtype classification accuracy [R17], which raises uncomfortable questions about whether the wave of newer deep factorisations and graph-learning frameworks actually improve on simpler baselines once evaluation is done outside the authors' own protocol. Third, methodological novelty continues to outpace reproducible software engineering: a model FAIR-packaged multi-omics workflow using Nextflow, containers, version control and rich metadata is described in [R27], illustrating what the general-purpose frameworks discussed here typically lack. Finally, the TCGA-centred benchmark culture is itself questionable — cancer cohorts are large, matched across modalities and well understood, which is the opposite of the regimes (small cohorts, block-missingness, single-cell resolution, non-model organisms) where many users actually work. Until the community invests in independent, domain-stratified benchmarking and treats software quality as a first-class scientific deliverable, comparative performance claims in this literature should be read with conspicuous caution.

Web servers and graphical interfaces occupy a critical niche in the multi-omics ecosystem by lowering the programming barrier for biologists and clinicians who would otherwise be excluded from integrative analysis. The Analyst suite, with its linked components for metabolomics (MetaboAnalyst [R7]), general omics (ExpressAnalyst, OmicsAnalyst) and knowledge-driven network integration (OmicsNet), exemplifies the design philosophy of providing a structured analytical path from raw data through single-omics analyses to joint dimensionality reduction and biological network interpretation [R23]. By formalising the workflow in a Nature Protocols contribution [R23], the developers frame accessibility as contingent not only on a friendly interface but also on transparent documentation of each analytical step, embedding reproducibility as a prerequisite for clinical translation. MetaboAnalyst 6.0 in particular extends metabolomics single-omics analysis with MS2 fragment-level annotation, complex multi-factor designs and metabolite–phenotype causal inference, while remaining operable entirely through a browser [R7]; this breadth makes it a frequent first stop in microbiome multi-omics pipelines where host or microbial metabolites carry substantial interpretive weight.

A parallel ecosystem has grown around the microbiome community. In practice, a 16S or metagenomic analysis has often required combining QIIME 2 [R8] for upstream processing, phyloseq [R6] for taxonomic object handling, and bespoke R scripts for differential abundance; MicrobiomeAnalyst [R9] offers a browser-accessible consolidation of these steps for 16S marker-gene and shotgun metagenomic/metatranscriptomic data. Its reliance on community-standard knowledge bases and statistical routines has supported rapid uptake by groups lacking dedicated bioinformaticians. Yet, as with MetaboAnalyst, the depth of integration is best characterised as a curated slice of well-established methods rather than a complete reimplementation of the underlying statistical machinery; the user is implicitly committed to the developers' choice of normalisation, transformation and multiple-testing correction. Differential-abundance testing on the metagenomics side is dominated by dedicated methods such as MaAsLin2 [R62] and ANCOM-BC [R63], which are typically called from command-line R sessions rather than through MicrobiomeAnalyst's interface; the Analyst suite thus occupies a complementary rather than substitutive niche for power users. Shifting from a browser GUI to a programmatic R workflow, EMP [R1] exposes microbiome multi-omics through SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment containers and organises its pipeline into five modules — extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation — articulated in a natural-language-style interface [R1]. The trade-off in accessibility this implies relative to the Analyst suite is offset by the deliberate unification of storage across omics layers and by the integration of microbiome-specific functionality that the upstream QIIME 2 [R8] and phyloseq [R6] toolchain otherwise leaves the user to assemble; the residual limitation, in our assessment, is that EMP does not in itself replace either the breadth of QIIME 2's upstream processing or the depth of single-object analyses that phyloseq has accumulated over more than a decade of community use.

General-purpose web and Streamlit-based platforms have proliferated recently. Profiler [R16] presents itself as an open-source, modular Python/Streamlit suite spanning proteomics, transcriptomics, lipidomics and even EEG data, integrating quality control, statistics, machine and deep learning, biomarker discovery, pathway enrichment and survival modelling. Its offer of the same environment both as a hosted web service and as a local container represents a notable step beyond the typical server-only deployment. Similarly, MuSA [R41] exposes the MultiAssayExperiment data structure through a Shiny interface specifically tailored to radiogenomic datasets — currently demonstrated on breast cancer cohorts — allowing researchers without R proficiency to perform pre-processing, correlation, clustering and feature selection on heterogeneous radiomic and molecular layers. The single-cell analyst [R20] supports six single-cell omics modalities (scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, scImmune profiling, single-cell copy number variation, cytometry by time-of-flight and flow cytometry) together with spatial transcriptomics, providing over 20 interactive tools that run in the browser.

Network-oriented multi-omics has its own dedicated platforms. MONGKIE [R46] pioneered integrated network visualisation and analysis for glioblastoma multi-omics by combining a Java-based visualisation unit with clustering and over-representation algorithms, enabling interactive mining that static command-line workflows struggle to match. NOODAI [R51] formalises a network-based pipeline in which representative differentially abundant or expressed traits from each omics layer seed a joint interaction network analysed by the MONET decomposition tool, revealing central elements that bridge omics layers. Disease-specific portals extend this logic to clinical translation, exemplified by CPMOAD [R22], which integrates uniformly processed RNA-seq, DNA methylation and curated interaction data for preeclampsia with interactive differential-expression, methylation and pathway-enrichment modules. Such platforms demonstrate that accessible interfaces can serve as stable supplementary-material repositories, allowing the figures and tables generated in the underlying study to be regenerated and inspected interactively long after publication.

The accessibility-versus-depth trade-off, however, is real and largely unresolved. Web implementations typically reimplement a thin statistical slice of published algorithms, often without preserving the original authors' exact default parameters or convergence diagnostics. Version drift is acute: a tool running today may not implement the same parameters as the version on which a published study was based, and the absence of immutable containerised builds means that figures rarely survive bit-perfectly into the reproducibility record. Most platforms also impose practical data-size limits — Profiler, MetaboAnalyst and MicrobiomeAnalyst all warn that inputs beyond tens of thousands of features or large single-cell matrices must be summarised or batched upstream — and uncertainty quantification is either absent or reduced to crude permutation heuristics rather than the Bayesian or bootstrap procedures available in dedicated R or Python frameworks such as MOFA+ [R4] or mixOmics [R3]. Containerised local deployment, which would mitigate many of these concerns, remains the exception: Profiler is one of the few to offer both web and desktop endpoints [R16], while CPMOAD [R22] and NOODAI [R51] rely on a hosted service model that cannot be replicated offline. Standardised multi-omics workflows built on Snakemake or Nextflow (workflow managers that orchestrate containerised analysis steps) provide a partial counterweight, exemplified by the FAIR Digital Object pipeline of Niehues et al. [R27] and the gNOMO host–microbiome pipeline [R43], but these target computational researchers rather than point-and-click users. The evidence therefore does not show that any single web platform provides the methodological depth of a dedicated command-line framework; what it does demonstrate is that such platforms are indispensable for reproducible supplementary material, for rapid clinical-translation pipelines where turnaround time matters more than algorithmic nuance, and as on-ramps that bring experimentalists into the multi-omics conversation before they graduate to programmatic workflows.

A broader tool census is worth flagging here even when not all entries are described in detail above. Seurat [R61] remains the dominant programmatic environment for single-cell integration, with its anchor-based strategy used across scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq and multimodal single-cell assays; in the benchmark of Hu et al. [R26] it is identified as one of six top performers, alongside totalVI, scArches, LS_Lab, MOJITOO and UINMF, with the caveat that the relative ranking is dataset-dependent — the same caveat that applies to integrative-clustering benchmarks such as Zhang et al. [R17], in which SNF gave the best subtype classification accuracy on TCGA colorectal cancer when benchmarked alongside seven competing unsupervised methods on simulated and real data, a finding whose generalisability is constrained by the choice of simulation regimes and tumour types examined. The mixOmics ecosystem provides multivariate multi-block alternatives, including DIABLO [R44], mixMC [R64] for compositional 16S data, and regularised generalised canonical correlation analysis (RGCCA [R65]) as one entry in a broader canonical-correlation family that also encompasses O2PLS and JIVE; these are typically driven from R rather than through web interfaces, with the earlier 3Omics web tool [R66] being a notable browser-based exception. For microbiome differential abundance, MaAsLin2 [R62] and ANCOM-BC [R63] have effectively become community standards and increasingly appear as modules inside integrative workflows. Anvi'o's interactive multi-omics visualisation platform is widely cited in microbial ecology and complements the integrative algorithms reviewed elsewhere in this manuscript, even though no dedicated card was available here to characterise it. PaintOmics occupies a similar pathway-level web niche and is not discussed in detail for the same reason. None of these tools addresses the same niche as the Analyst suite, but together they bracket the population of options a reader should weigh before committing to a particular web platform.
